lens: Senior front-end engineer, high-traffic e-commerce. Judged only on: is it buildable exactly as specified on the browser support the research pack documents; will it hold 60fps on a mid-range Android and a 3-year-old iPhone; what is the honest first-view payload in MB; does the liquid-glass degradation ladder actually survive Safari and Firefox; are the API costs/shapes stated correctly; where does a concept assert something the research contradicts; what are the accessibility failures; what is the real build effort. I ran every load-bearing contrast number through a WCAG calculator rather than taking any of them on trust.

strengths: Glass ladder is correct and correctly reasoned: Tier 2 is the product, Tier 1 gated by an engine probe rather than @supports (the research explicitly documents Firefox returning true and rendering nothing), colour-interpolation-filters="sRGB" called out as non-optional, filterUnits="userSpaceOnUse" with map regeneration on resize, both href and xlink:href on feImage. Nothing here assumes a capability the research says is missing.
Tier 3 floor uses plain rgb(15 15 15 / .94) — correct, because a browser old enough to lack backdrop-filter also lacks color-mix(). This is the only concept that gets the true floor right.
Sequence engineering is production-grade and matches the research line for line: canvas not scrubbed

Best accessibility primitive of the three: a real focus-ring spec that works on both themes (2px solid #FAF6F6, 2px offset, 4px #0F0F0F halo, swapped on paper) and is explicitly painted above the glass. Wordmark as outlined inline SVG with role=img and a <title> removes the word-space-collapse risk entirely rather than mitigating it.

Only concept that correctly polices Gemini's 6-object/5-character/3-style reference budget — it explicitly checks its two-model group shot against the 5-character cap and flags it as the highest-drift asset.
Refuses Lenis, Three.js and Hydrogen for the right documented reasons, and ships the ~60-line raw-WebGL depth plate instead of 185KB gz of scene graph.

Colourway `bg: dark | paper` field enforced in the catalogue schema is a genuinely good engineering answer to a palette-maths problem — it makes the constraint un-forgettable rather than a review note.
weaknesses: The 1.4MB mobile first-interaction budget is unachievable as specified. The cover is a full-bleed autoplaying 8s 1080×1920 H.264 loop; autoplay means the whole file downloads once it's in viewport, so the real first-view payload on a phone is ~2.5–4.5MB (video) + ~100KB AVIF poster + ~100KB of subset Söhne woff2 + CSS/JS, before the 2.0MB deferred sequence. The budget and the art direction contradict each other and the budget loses.

The AVIF hero poster is the LCP element. AVIF decodes 5–10× slower than JPEG (the research's own finding); on a Snapdragon 6-series that is 100–200ms added to LCP for no byte saving worth having at hero size. JPEG or WebP poster.

No costed pilot. The brief demands a cheap high-signal pilot that fits ~$15 with the full set costed separately, and this concept ships 13 assets with no arithmetic anywhere. Priced out as written (4K hero at $0.24, six-call colourway run, two Veo 1080p covers at $0.96 each, one 8s PDP loop per colourway) the specified set is roughly $18–30 before a single re-roll, and 3× re-roll on stills is the realistic rate. It does not demonstrably fit the budget.

The sticky collection filter bar is full-width, 48px tall, blur(10px), position:sticky, over a scrolling product grid. That is the same WebKit per-scroll-frame re-rasterisation case the concept spends 600 words avoiding for the nav, and it contradicts its own "blurred area × dpr² is the dominant term" argument. Small pill, giant bar.

Twelve distinct surfaces (7 home spreads + ledger + PDP + cart + drop + story) is the largest build of the three, with two of the spreads (the depth plate, the index image-swap) carrying bespoke code that appears exactly once.

The one-liner claims "the only moving thing on the site being a single slow specular sweep" while the spec ships an autoplay cover video, per-viewport settles, a WebGL parallax plate, a 120-frame pinned sequence and per-colourway PDP loops. Internal overclaim — minor, but it's the kind of gap that survives into the client conversation.
fatal_flaws: The contrast arithmetic the adaptive nav flip is built on is wrong, and it's presented as verified working. It claims a 0.78 dark scrim composited over #DFDDDE gives a background luminance of ~0.21 against which bone ink is 3.8:1 and fails, and concludes "the maths forces" the flip. Computed: 0.78×#0F0F0F over #DFDDDE = #3D3C3D, and #FAF6F6 on that is 10.24:1 — comfortably passing. The flip is a good aesthetic decision; it is not a legibility necessity, and the concept's single most-cited piece of engineering proof does not survive a calculator.

WCAG 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide (Level A) is named in the motion section as "a legal-exposure item" and then not implemented. The cover ships an indefinitely looping autoplay video with a text overlay and no pause control; the only escape is prefers-reduced-motion, which is a different user and a different requirement. For a UK commercial storefront that is an actual Level A failure on the first screen.

strengths: Best payload profile of the three by a wide margin, and it is structural rather than lucky. The above-the-fold hero is a canvas sequence, not a video — first view on mobile is one preloaded AVIF frame (~40–80KB) + wordmark SVG + subset fonts + ~15KB CSS + ~25KB JS, realistically under 500KB, with the 2.0MB sequence deferred past load + requestIdleCallback and dropped entirely under Save-Data or effectiveType 2g/3g. Concepts 1 and 3 both ship a multi-megabyte autoplay video above the fold on a phone; this one does not.

The one number that decides whether the sequence survives a mid-range Android is memory, and this is the only concept that scales the sliding window per tier as the research instructs (16 at 828, 8 at 1440, 24 at 540) *and* applies createImageBitmap resizeWidth on top. 108 MiB → ~40 MiB is stated with the working shown.

Every contrast claim it makes checks out to two decimal places: bone/ground 17.9 (17.87), grey/ground 7.8 (7.81), denim/ground 3.2 (3.196), bone-on-denim-fill 5.59 (5.591), and the catch that matters — washed black #171717 on #0F0F0F is 1.07:1 (1.0697). That last one is a genuine launch-saver and it drove an art-direction rule, not a CSS patch. I could not falsify a single number in this concept.

The .74 scrim floor holds under adversarial test: composited over pure white it still gives bone text 7.88:1, so the claim "legible regardless of what is behind the pill" is true, which is what makes blurring where the entire category doesn't defensible.

Solving the hardest documented collision (fixed + backdrop-filter over a per-frame-repainting canvas, worst case on iOS) by making the nav go solid for the duration of the pin — via an opacity cross-fade of two pre-blurred layers, never a transitioning blur radius — and then using that same switch as the concept's narrative punctuation. The perf fix and the art direction are the same line of code. That is the best single engineering decision in any of the three.

Only concept with an itemised pilot that fits the stated ceiling: $8.75 against $15, priced at the research's actual rates ($0.134 per 1K/2K Gemini image, $0.24 at 4K, Veo 3.1 Fast 720p $0.10/s → $0.80 per 8s take), with a 3× re-roll allowance built in and the full set costed separately at ~$36. I re-did the arithmetic; it's right. It also correctly notes the Blender sequence costs $0 in API spend, which is precisely why the budget works.

API shapes are correct where the others slip: Veo called via predictLongRunning with aspectRatio/durationSeconds-as-string/resolution/personGeneration=allow_adult, image and lastFrame both set to the same PNG for a seamless loop, 48h URI expiry handled in-run, audio stripped with -an because it cannot be disabled and is billed regardless. Gemini reference budget respected.

Correct px-per-frame arithmetic at both breakpoints (260vh desktop → ~11.7px/frame, 220vh mobile → ~7.8px/frame), both inside the research's stated comfort bands. The only concept whose scroll-runway maths I could reproduce.
weaknesses: Tier 3 — the universal floor — is written as `background: color-mix(in oklab, #0F0F0F 92%, transparent)`. Any engine old enough to lack backdrop-filter also lacks color-mix (Safari 16.2+, Chrome 111+), so the declaration is dropped and the true floor is a transparent pill with bone text on arbitrary photography. It inherited this from the research brief's own example; concepts 1 and 3 both use plain rgba and are correct. One-line fix, but it is the one tier that exists specifically for the case where nothing else works.

The cart drawer spec contains no focus trap, no Escape handler and no focus-return-to-trigger — the only one of the three to omit all three. On mobile it becomes an 88svh bottom sheet "with a drag handle", which is a pointer-only affordance with no stated keyboard equivalent. That is a straightforward WCAG 2.1.2 / 2.4.3 failure in the highest-value surface on the site.

No WCAG 2.2.2 pause control on the autoplaying lookbook loop, despite naming SC 2.2.2 as "baseline legal exposure for a UK storefront" in the motion section. Same gap as concept 1: reduced-motion handling is wired, a pause mechanism is not.

Renaming SOLD OUT to "TIME'S UP" and restock to "BACK ON THE CLOCK" is a comprehension and conversion risk, and it collides with the sparse-variant matrix it correctly models elsewhere: a struck chip means "never made", a TIME'S UP chip means "sold out", and the customer now has two non-standard signals to decode on the same row. Screen-reader output becomes "TIME'S UP" with no availability semantics attached.

The pre-hero wordmark overlay is an unnecessary risk surface: a full-bleed opaque layer over the LCP image, dismissed on a decode() promise, gated on sessionStorage. It won't break LCP (inline SVG paths aren't LCP candidates and the beneath retains opacity 1), but it is a page-load intro animation on the teardown's own ban list, and it is the kind of thing that shows as a white flash on a cold cache.

260vh/220vh of pinned scroll is the whole homepage narrative, so iOS pin debugging (URL-bar show/hide, rubber-band, ScrollTrigger refresh on resize) is on the critical path rather than in a side section. The concept says so honestly, which is to its credit, but it is still a single point of failure.
Like the other two it budgets GSAP at ~27KB gz. That is the core bundle; the research says ScrollTrigger is roughly 11KB on top. Real dynamic-import cost is ~38KB gz.

strengths: The only concept that actually ships a WCAG 2.2.2 pause control: "A 10px PAUSE control bottom-right (WCAG 2.2.2, Level A)" on the autoplaying hero. The other two name the criterion and then don't implement it. On a UK commercial storefront that is the difference between a compliance item and a compliance failure.

Best alt-text and state discipline: explicitly distinct alt per gallery image with a worked example, SOLD OUT kept literal rather than brand-voiced, and three genuinely distinct size-chip states (available / sold out / does not exist in this colourway) with aria-disabled and an inline NOTIFY reveal. Also correct on quantityAvailable:null meaning untracked, not zero.
Tier 3 floor is plain rgb(15 15 15 / .93) — correct, unlike concept 2.

Bottom-anchoring the pill on mobile is a real conversion argument (thumb arc) and it does move the blur off the hero video for most of the session — the reasoning is sound even though the execution is where it comes apart.

Correct on the expensive fundamentals: canvas not scrubbed video, behind the canvas as the LCP candidate, createImageBitmap with resizeWidth, window scaled to tier, rAF coalescing, boot after load, no Three.js, no Lenis, opacity cross-fade rather than animating blur radius, Hydrogen rejected.

A Playwright assertion that measures the rendered gap between the R and the T in the wordmark and fails the build under 0.5em is the single best piece of CI thinking in any of the three — it turns the brief's stated fragility into a gate rather than a promise.

Commercially the sharpest: quick-add on the card, sold-out timestamps, dispatch cutoff as a second timer in a different register, free-shipping progress in the drawer, JSON-LD with priceValidUntil tied to the drop close.
weaknesses: Claims #FAF6F6 on #0F0F0F is 19.1:1. It is 17.87:1. Small, but it is presented as a measured value in a palette section whose authority rests on everything having been measured.

The SSR justification is half wrong. Reason (1) — "product pages must be server-rendered for Product JSON-LD and indexable PDPs — a client-only SPA storefront is an SEO own-goal" — conflates SSG with SPA. Astro's static output produces fully indexable PDPs with JSON-LD. Only reason (2) (private Storefront token for metaobjects must stay server-side) is real, and it is conditional on a decision not yet made. The concept therefore commits to a runtime, an edge deploy and an ops surface it admits "the owner cannot maintain", on a justification that is 50% incorrect.

The Veo request is written as "Veo 3.1 Fast, 1080x1920 and 1920x1080" — the Gemini API takes aspectRatio ("9:16"/"16:9") plus resolution ("1080p"), not pixel dimensions. The per-take cost ($0.96 at Fast 1080p) is right; the call shape is not.

No itemised pilot. "~£13 pilot, ~£70 full" appears once in the risks with no working. Better than concept 1, materially worse than concept 2, and the brief specifically asked for a plan that demonstrably survives a $15 ceiling.

2px grid gutters at 2-up on a 390px viewport puts six always-visible size chips inside a ~187px card — ~31px per chip. It clears the 24px WCAG 2.5.8 AA minimum and nothing more; it will be a mis-tap generator on the site's primary conversion affordance.

Self-contradicts on the focus ring: the palette section says "not focus rings (those are bone)", the glass section says "Focus rings sit above the glass, solid --ot-live 2px with a 2px bone offset". Both are defensible; shipping both is not.

"SOLD OUT — 23:14, SUN 12 OCT" is a good idea that needs a data source the concept never names. Shopify does not expose a sold-out timestamp through the Storefront API; it would have to be captured by a webhook into your own store and surfaced through the ContentAdapter. Buildable, but it is unbudgeted work presented as free ("it costs nothing because the platform already stores it" — it doesn't, not where the front end can read it).
fatal_flaws: The morphing bottom-anchored glass pill is the riskiest single component proposed in any of the three, and it is the site's core mechanic so it cannot be cut. It stacks every documented hazard at once: position:fixed + backdrop-filter (WebKit recomputes the blur every scroll frame, does not reproduce on desktop); bottom-anchored with env(safe-area-inset-bottom) on iOS, where the URL-bar collapse/expand changes the inset mid-scroll and fixed bottom elements visibly jump; and then a 320ms "shared-element width/content transition" that animates the *geometry* of a backdrop-filtered element, which invalidates the blur cache on every frame of the morph — the one thing the research says never to do, in a different costume. On a PDP at 360px it then has to hold [S][M][L][XL][XXL] plus "ADD — £48" in a full-width-minus-gutters pill; with the six-size run the brief's range implies, that overflows.

The hero sequence (S01) rests on a compositing claim that will not work as described: animate the sand inside the print region of a single still and displace the fill line "by the depth map so the sand line follows the fabric folds and breaks at the crease". Monocular depth estimation (Depth Anything V2) produces smooth, low-frequency scene depth — it does not resolve garment folds at print scale. The correct displacement source is a luminance/normal derivation from the photograph itself. As specified this either produces a flat sticker sliding over a photo, or 4–6 days of unplanned hand-rotoscoping with an uncertain outcome — and it is the entire 3D-flair budget and the structural payoff of the page.

The group frame E01-CREW passes ten character reference images ("Images 1–5 and 6–10 are CHARACTER references for two different adults") plus three garment plus three style. Gemini 3 Pro Image caps at 5 character, 6 object, 3 style, 14 total. This request is over the character cap by 2× and over the total cap. Concept 1 checks this exact constraint explicitly and stays inside it; this one will 400 or silently drop references on the most expensive frame in its asset list.

The error state is specified as "bone text on a #171717 chip with a 2px --ot-live left rule" on a #0F0F0F ground. #171717 on #0F0F0F is 1.07:1 — the chip is invisible. The concept establishes the "#171717 never on the ground" rule itself, two sections earlier, and then breaks it in the one component whose entire job is to be noticed.

best_ideas_to_graft.idea: The visible PAUSE control on the autoplaying hero loop, and keeping SOLD OUT as literal text rather than brand voice.
best_ideas_to_graft.why: WCAG 2.2.2 Pause/Stop/Hide is Level A and applies to any auto-starting motion over 5 seconds — prefers-reduced-motion does not discharge it. THE COUNTER is the only concept that ships the control. Graft it onto every autoplaying element in the winner (the lookbook loop and the PDP loops), and drop 'TIME'S UP'/'BACK ON THE CLOCK' in favour of literal availability strings so the sparse-variant matrix stays legible to a screen reader and to a first-time shopper.

best_ideas_to_graft.idea: The Playwright CI assertion that measures the rendered pixel gap between the R and the T in the OUR TIME wordmark and fails the build below 0.5em.
best_ideas_to_graft.why: The brief names the word space as the fragile part. Both other concepts protect it by shipping the wordmark as outlined SVG, which is right — but live type still appears in <title>, og:title, alt text and the newsletter line. A build gate is the only thing that catches a regression there, and it costs about an hour.

best_ideas_to_graft.idea: The explicit dual-theme focus-ring token (2px solid ink, 2px offset, 4px ground halo, colours swapped on paper, always painted above the glass) and the catalogue-level `bg: dark | paper` field per colourway.
best_ideas_to_graft.why: The winner's accessibility spec is thinner than its perf spec. A solid, never-translucent focus ring specified once as a token is the cheapest way to make a glass-heavy site keyboard-usable, and the bg field turns the 1.07:1 washed-black finding — which the winner discovered — into a schema constraint that can't be forgotten in month six.

best_ideas_to_graft.idea: Tier 3 written with plain rgb(15 15 15 / .94) rather than color-mix(), and the explicit Gemini 6-object/5-character/3-style budget check on every multi-reference call.
best_ideas_to_graft.why: Two direct bug fixes for the winner. Its Tier 3 uses color-mix, which is unsupported in exactly the engines Tier 3 exists to serve, so the floor evaporates in the only case it's needed. And THE SLOW HAND's habit of auditing reference-slot counts per call is what stops the most expensive asset in the shoot from 400ing.

best_ideas_to_graft.idea: Time-first information architecture on /shop — chronological default sort with category, colour and size as filters applied on top, plus the per-image mono dateline carrying a real date and place.
best_ideas_to_graft.why: The winner's collection page is competent but conventional. Chronological-first IA is free to implement (it's a default sort order and a `publishedAt` field already in the domain model), it scales to drop 02/03/04 without a redesign, and the dateline system answers the teardown's 'no real numbers, no real dates, no real place names' tell with zero runtime cost.

best_ideas_to_graft.idea: The dispatch-cutoff timer rendered server-side per request, and the sold-out timestamp — but budget the webhook that captures it.
best_ideas_to_graft.why: Two timers in two registers is the thing that stops a countdown reading as a Shopify app, and the winner already has the hype timer. Take the service timer too, but bring THE SLOW HAND's correction with it: render the cutoff server-side with the right BST/GMT offset rather than ticking it in the client, so there is no jitter and no hydration mismatch. And if the sold-out timestamp is wanted, cost the order webhook — it is not free from the Storefront API.

verdict:
THE GLASS EMPTIES wins, and it wins on the two things that actually kill fashion sites on real phones: payload above the fold, and what happens when the glass meets moving content.

**Payload.** It is the only one of the three whose first screen on a phone is not a multi-megabyte autoplay video. THE SLOW HAND and THE COUNTER both open on a full-bleed 8s 1080p loop, which downloads in full the moment it enters viewport; realistic first-view weight on a mid-range Android is 2.5–4.5MB before anything deferred, and THE SLOW HAND states a 1.4MB budget it cannot meet with its own hero. THE GLASS EMPTIES opens on a single preloaded AVIF frame behind the canvas — call it 400–500KB all in (frame + subset woff2 + ~15KB CSS + ~25KB JS), with a 2.0MB sequence deferred past `load` and suppressed entirely under Save-Data or effectiveType 2g/3g. On the research's own UK cellular figures (3–8 Mbps real-world) that is the difference between a 1.5s LCP and a 4s one.

**The glass.** All three get the ladder architecturally right — Tier 2 is the product, Tier 1 is engine-gated rather than `@supports`-gated (correct, because Firefox returns true and renders nothing), `color-interpolation-filters="sRGB"` is flagged as non-optional, `userSpaceOnUse` with regeneration on resize. None of them assumes refraction works in WebKit. But THE GLASS EMPTIES is the only one that makes the hardest collision — `position: fixed` + `backdrop-filter` over a per-frame-repainting canvas, the worst case on iOS — into a design beat rather than a mitigation, by going solid for the duration of the pin via an opacity cross-fade of two pre-blurred layers. THE SLOW HAND does the same thing and calls it "a genuine loss, not a clever solve". It isn't a loss; it's the right answer, and the concept that frames it as intent will ship it without argument.

**Arithmetic.** I ran every load-bearing contrast claim. THE GLASS EMPTIES is clean to two decimals on all of them (17.9, 7.8, 3.2, 5.59, and the 1.07:1 washed-black-on-ground catch that genuinely saves a launch), and its 0.74 scrim floor holds under adversarial test — composited over pure white, bone text is still 7.88:1. THE COUNTER claims 19.1:1 where the answer is 17.9. THE SLOW HAND's is worse than a rounding error: it claims a 0.78 dark scrim over the paper section leaves bone ink at 3.8:1 and therefore that "the maths forces" the adaptive nav flip. The real figure is 10.24:1. The flip is still good design, but the one piece of engineering proof that concept leans hardest on does not survive a calculator, and I have to weight that.

**Cost and API accuracy.** THE GLASS EMPTIES is the only concept that costs the pilot at all: $8.75 itemised against the $15 ceiling, at the research's actual rates, with a 3× re-roll allowance and the full set priced separately at ~$36. The arithmetic is correct. Its Veo calls are the right shape (predictLongRunning, `aspectRatio`, `durationSeconds` as a string, `personGeneration: "allow_adult"` for UK image-conditioned generation, audio stripped with `-an` because it cannot be disabled and is billed regardless, 48h URI expiry handled in-run). THE COUNTER writes Veo requests with pixel dimensions where the API takes an aspect ratio, and passes ten character references to Gemini against a documented cap of five. THE SLOW HAND has no budget anywhere; priced as written its asset list is $18–30 before re-rolls.

**Why not THE COUNTER**, which is commercially the sharpest and has the best accessibility instincts of the three: its core mechanic is a bottom-anchored glass pill that *morphs* — a 320ms geometry transition on a `backdrop-filter` element, which invalidates the blur cache on every frame of the morph, on a fixed bottom element whose `env(safe-area-inset-bottom)` shifts mid-scroll as the iOS URL bar collapses, and which then has to hold six size chips plus a price at 360px. That is three documented hazards stacked in the one component that cannot be cut. Its hero sequence rests on displacing sand by a monocular depth map "so the fill line follows the fabric folds" — depth maps are smooth and low-frequency and will not resolve folds at print scale; that's either a flat sticker or a week of unplanned rotoscoping. And it puts its error chip at #171717 on #0F0F0F (1.07:1, invisible) two sections after writing the rule forbidding it.

**Honest build effort**, one senior dev, design signed off, excluding asset generation:
- Shared core all three need (tokens + hand-written CSS, Astro scaffold, commerce domain + adapter + local-JSON + conformance suite, collection, PDP, cart drawer, SEO/JSON-LD, a11y pass, real-device QA): **22–26 days.**
- THE GLASS EMPTIES adds 8 bespoke home sections, the Blender hourglass (3–4 days including match-cut iteration against the photograph), the WebGL depth plate (1.5 days), the first-paint overlay, and iOS pin debugging (1–2 days, and budget for it to be 3): **+11–14 days → 33–40 dev days, ~7–8 weeks.**
- THE SLOW HAND: **36–44 dev days, ~8–9 weeks** — twelve surfaces, two of them carrying code used once.
- THE COUNTER: **35–43 dev days, ~7–9 weeks**, with by far the highest variance, because the morphing pill is 3–4 days on its own and the sand comp is 4–6 days that may produce nothing usable.

Add 6–8 days of asset generation and QA to all three; the research is right that the rejection rate, not the API spend, is the real cost.

**Three fixes before THE GLASS EMPTIES goes to build, all cheap:** rewrite Tier 3 with plain `rgba` (a browser without `backdrop-filter` also lacks `color-mix`, so the universal floor currently evaporates in the one case it exists for); add a focus trap, Escape handler and focus-return to the cart drawer, plus a keyboard path for the mobile bottom sheet's drag handle; and ship a visible pause control on every autoplaying loop. Then re-budget GSAP honestly at ~38KB gz — all three concepts quote 27KB, which is the core bundle, not core plus ScrollTrigger.
